context: Saint Bernard is speaking. His prayer, announced in the last line of Canto 32, runs to line 39: first praise of Mary, then the request that she win for Dante the sight of God.

note: One of the poem's most famous lines: "Vergine Madre, figlia del tuo figlio". It is built on paradoxes. Mary is both virgin and mother, and as a creature she is the daughter of the God she bore.
God chose her from eternity, before the world was made, as the one through whom he would enter it.

quote: to become what He had made
note: The Incarnation: God the maker became a human being, one of his own creatures, by being born of Mary.

context: The Rose exists because of Mary. The love between God and humankind, cold since Adam's sin, was lit again in her womb, and that warmth made the flower of the saved grow.

note: To the blessed, who already have what they hoped for, she is love at its brightest. To the living, who do not yet have it, she is a spring of hope.
As it did for Dante himself. In Inferno 2 Mary saw him lost in the dark wood and sent help before he had asked for any.
Dante. Bernard sums up the whole journey in three lines: from the bottom of Hell, at the center of the earth, up to this point.
The souls of Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, whose conditions he has seen one after another.
God himself. To see God directly is what theologians call the beatific vision, the happiness of the saved.
Dante is still a living man in a mortal body, and that dims his sight. Bernard asks Mary to clear it away.
Dante must go back to earth and live out his life. Bernard asks that he stay faithful afterward, and that the vision not be wasted on him.

context: Her last appearance in the poem: one of the blessed among the rest, her hands joined in prayer for him.

note: Mary's eyes. She gives no spoken answer. She looks at Bernard to show the prayer is granted, then turns her gaze to God.
No created being, human or angel, sees as deeply into God as Mary does.
God, the good that every desire is really seeking, and in which desire comes to rest.
Dante's verb can mean either that his longing rose to its highest point or that it came to an end, satisfied. Commentators are divided, and the translation takes the first reading.

context: His last act as guide. From here Dante has no guide and needs none: he is alone before God.

note: God's light alone is true in itself. Every other truth is a reflection of it.

quote: greater than our language can express
note: From here to the end, Dante says again and again that words and memory both fail him. He does not describe God. He describes what it was like to try to see, and what little stayed with him.
The first of three images for forgetting: a dream whose mood lingers after its content is gone, snow losing its shape in the sun, and leaves blown away by wind.
The Sibyl of Cumae, a prophetess in Virgil's Aeneid, wrote her answers on leaves and laid them in order in her cave. When the door opened the wind scattered them, and their meaning was lost.
The purpose of the whole poem in a phrase: to carry back one spark of what he saw, for readers not yet born.

quote: if I had turned my eyes away
note: The reverse of earthly light. Looking at the sun damages the eye, but looking at this light strengthens it, and only looking away would have left him dazed.

The first thing he sees in God. Everything that exists is like the loose pages of a book, scattered through the universe. In God they are gathered and bound by love into one volume. The image is one of the most admired in the poem.

Terms from the philosophy of Aristotle, used in the medieval schools. A substance is a thing that exists in its own right, such as a man or a tree. Accidents are features that exist only in a thing, such as its color or size. Together they cover everything there is.
The binding together of all things in God. He cannot recall the sight itself, and trusts that he had it only because his joy grows as he speaks of it.
A difficult comparison, much debated. The usual reading: one moment after the vision has made him forget more of it than twenty-five centuries have made the world forget of the voyage of the Argo.

The Argo, in which Jason sailed for the Golden Fleece, was said to be the first ship. Neptune, the god of the sea, looks up amazed from the seabed as the shadow of its hull passes overhead: something never seen before. Dante's own amazement before God is the same.

quote: the good that is the object of the will
note: The will wants only what it sees as good. God is all good gathered in one, so a soul that sees him cannot want to look anywhere else.
The poet at the height of his power compares his speech to a baby's babbling at the breast. Images of infancy run through these last cantos.

quote: kept transforming as I myself changed
note: God does not change. Dante's sight grows stronger as he looks, so he sees more and more in the same light. The three visions that follow are stages of his seeing, not changes in God.

context: Three circles of three colors and one size, occupying the same space: three distinct persons who are one God. Dante gives a geometer's figure, and says at once that it falls short.

note: The Father and the Son. The Son comes from the Father as a second rainbow is thrown off by the first in a double rainbow: light from light, as the creed says.
The Holy Spirit, the love between Father and Son. The Western Church taught that the Spirit proceeds from both of them equally.
Three lines that pack in the theology of the Trinity. God alone fully knows himself. The Father is God knowing, the Son is God known, and the Spirit is the love and joy that pass between them.
The second circle, the Son.
A human figure appears within the circle of the Son, in the circle's own color. This is the Incarnation, the second great mystery of the faith: Christ is fully God and fully human at once.

A famous ancient problem: to construct a square with exactly the same area as a given circle. Geometers had tried for centuries and failed, and it was proved impossible in 1882. A circle and a square will not measure each other, and neither, for the human mind, will God and man.

quote: how the image fit the circle
note: How a human nature can be joined to the divine nature in one person. Dante can see that it is so, but not how.
Understanding is given to him in an instant, by grace and not by his own effort. He does not say what he understood. The poem's climax is left unspoken.
In Italian, "l'alta fantasia": the power of the mind to form images, which has carried the poem this far. Past this point nothing can be pictured, so the poem must stop.
A wheel turning evenly, every part moving at one pace. Dante's desire and his will now move together and in step with God's love. The vision ends in being changed, more than in knowing.

quote: the Love that moves the sun and all the stars
note: The last line of the Comedy: "l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle". God is named as the love that turns the universe, and Dante is now turning with it. Each of the three parts of the poem ends on the same word, stelle, stars.
